extracted.intended_audience: general readers, taxpayers, students and readers of political economy, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for assessing economic actions and public policy decisions, emphasizing visible versus hidden consequences, opportunity costs, and distributional effects using concrete examples (machinery, credit, public spending, saving vs luxury).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider both 'what is seen' and 'what is not seen'
rubrics_metrics.description: Always examine both the immediate, visible effects of an action ("that which is seen") and the indirect, less visible or delayed consequences ("that which is not seen").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated throughout: when a new machine dismisses workers this is "what is seen"; the subsequent savings, lower prices, reallocated spending and new employment opportunities are "what is not seen". Apply this test to machinery, credit, public expenditure, colonization, and private spending vs saving. Examples: James B. saving a franc by using a machine (seen: one fewer worker; not seen: the saved franc employs another worker elsewhere); public works in Algeria (seen: houses and ports built; not seen: private expenditures and employments foregone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse money (cash/paper) with real production
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing credit, loans, or monetary interventions, evaluate the physical productions (ploughs, houses, tools) that money represents rather than focusing on money itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Forget money, coin, bills" — treat money as a medium; a loan does not create additional real goods beyond what lenders can supply. Example: a farmer borrowing fifty francs receives a plough (a production), not abstract money that increases the country's stock of goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit/distributional interventions displace credit, they do not create production
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions of credit and State guarantees facilitate matching borrowers and lenders but cannot increase the total amount of real capital or productions available at a given time; they merely displace who receives loans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State security for loans may increase the number of borrowers but does not increase lenders or total available goods; it can raise interest rates and transfer burdens to taxpayers. Example thought experiment: only one plough exists—State guaranteeing James's loan means John loses access to it; the operation displaces credit rather than augmenting it, and can cause injustice to original lenders/credit-worthy borrowers.

rubrics_metrics.name: When evaluating public expenditure, account for opportunity cost and redistributed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess public spending not only by visible employment and works produced but by the private expenditures and benefits that are prevented when taxes are raised to pay for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public projects (e.g., building ports/roads in Algeria) show visible benefits where money is spent (construction, trade in Marseilles) but obscure the private consumption, repairs, investments, and local employment across the rest of the country that taxation has suppressed. Always deduct the harm caused by preventing private expense from the apparent public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public spending can concentrate and displace labor geographically and economically
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective expenditures that accumulate resources at a point attract displaced labour and disturb the natural distribution of population and trades, often producing a feverish but fragile activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the State draws 50,000,000 francs and spends them in one region, that attracts labor from many parishes and paralyzes employment elsewhere; when the fund is exhausted the concentrated activity can turn into a problem. Consider longer-term sustainability and distributional consequences, not just immediate local stimulus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saving is (ultimately) another form of spending — evaluate long-term effects of frugality vs luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic assessment should recognize that prudent saving channels resources into capital formation and future productive spending; moral virtue of frugality aligns with public interest because it increases national capital and future demand for labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast Mondor (prodigal spender) with Aristus (economical saver): both circulate money in the economy, but Aristus's savings are invested or lent and produce a growing, sustainable fund for wages and investment. Do not judge economic impact only by immediate visible consumption; trace saved funds into investments, sales of land/rents, loans, and subsequent expenditures.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-provided work or profit rights paid by taxation displace privately funded work/profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs promising employment or protected profits financed by taxpayers substitute for private-sector labor and demand; public provision financed by taxation does not create net additional work but reallocates whose funds pay for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: national workshops (1848) paid from taxpayers reduced private consumption (forty-five centimes) and thus reduced demand for tailors, carpenters, etc. Protectionist subsidies that make a trade profitable transfer losses onto others. Principle: "two kinds of meal cannot come out of one sack."

rubrics_metrics.name: When judging government proposals, always identify and examine the resource trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Any expansion of Government activity requires resources (taxes); proposals must be evaluated in light of where those resources come from and what they prevent, not merely for their visible goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Government is besieged with conflicting demands (organize labour, colonize, instruct youth, assist aged, etc.); but each program needs funding. Citizens will object when taxes disable their own projects (repairing houses, manuring fields). Insist on clear accounting of who pays and what private actions are displaced.
